# The many faces of Indra

No important name has only one face. **Indra** appears ​as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and a digital temple. This post looks at each face in ‌turn: the name and its roots, the Devanagari original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the symbols and sanctuaries, and the afterlife that brought the canonical spelling into the present.

## At ‌a Glance

- **Restored name:** Indra
- **ASCII form:** indra
- **Meaning:** "the god of the atmosphere and sky"
- **Domain of influence:** Storms, War, Kingship
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** ​इन्द्र (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Indra** (*indra*) — The Storm, the Vajra, King of the Gods · the god of the atmosphere and sky — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where ​it is catalogued under the domain "Storms, War, Kingship". The name means "the god of the atmosphere and sky".

**Indra** is the king of the Vedic gods: the thunderbolt-bearer ​who slew the dragon Vritra and released the rivers, the drinker of soma who roars into battle, the thousand-eyed lord of the sky. Two hundred and fifty hymns ​of the Rigveda are addressed to him — more than to any other deity — making him the best-documented god of the ancient world.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly ​spelling **Indra** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/indra/). The plain ASCII form *indra* contains ‌the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## The Name

The name is attested in ​Devanagari as **इन्द्र**. Etymologically it means "the god of the atmosphere and sky".

The canonical spelling **Indra** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *indra* contains ​the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. The editorial work is to fix one reviewed reference spelling, preserve capitalization and provenance, and keep the ‌original evidence visible. ## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as ‌**इन्द्र**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Indra*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Indra is written in Devanagari as इन्द्र
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to ​a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈɪndrə/** ‌— Sanskrit (IAST: Indra).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **In-** — Short i as in “bit”, followed by the retroflex dental n — tongue curled back.
- **-dra** — The d is ​retroflex ḍ in careful speech; the final a is a light schwa, half-sounded.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “IN-druh” — the final vowel breathes rather ​than lands

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Vedic** — Índra
- **Pāli/Prakrit** — Inda
- **Buddhist** — Śakra

One of the oldest named gods in any Indo-European language — ​the name appears already in the Rigveda’s first hymn.

## Mythology

The Indra of the Rigveda is a storm in divine form: mighty, boisterous, sometimes embarrassed, always central. His one ​great myth — the combat with Vritra — is the Vedic creation story: the waters of life imprisoned by the dragon, the thunderbolt that splits the mountains, the rivers ​released. Everything else in his mythology is commentary on that victory.

### The Slaying of Vritra (Rigveda 1.32)

Vritra, the “Enveloper”, coiled about the world’s waters and held them ‌fast in his mountain caves. Indra, armed with the vajra forged by Tvashtri from Dadhichi’s bones, struck the dragon on its flank; the waters burst free and flooded to ​the sea. ‘Like lowing cows the waters rushed’ — the oldest dragon-slaying in recorded literature, and the template for every one after it.

### The Drink of Soma (Rigveda 8)

‌Before the combat, Indra drinks three lakes of soma pressed by the priests; filled with the draught, his strength is irresistible and his belly vast. The hymns taunt and ​flatter him by turns — the Vedic poets knew their storm-god was vain, and loved him for it. Soma is both his fuel and his fee.

### The Intoxication ‌Hymn (Rigveda 10.119)

The most human hymn in the Rigveda: Indra speaks in the first person, drunk on soma, boasting — ‘I will break the earth’s two halves apart, ​like a gourd I will break the two worlds’. The gods’ king, for one hymn, sounds like a warrior at the feast, and the poets let him.

### From King ‌of Gods to Dethroned Elder (Epic & Purāṇic Cycle)

In the later epics the balance shifts: Vishnu’s avatars take the great victories, and Indra becomes the anxious king who ​sins — the seducer of Ahalyā, the raider of Triparu, the god who must yield his throne’s preeminence. The Purāṇas preserve a dignity-muted Indra, still lord of the ‌eastern quarter and of the storm, but no longer the cosmos’ protagonist.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Indra concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each ​a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Vajra** — The thunderbolt forged from the bones of the sage Dadhichi — Indra’s irresistible weapon against the dragon.
- **Slayer of Vritra** ​— He split the dragon that held the waters captive, and the rivers ran free — the founding victory of cosmic order.
- **Lord of Soma** — The sacred draught ‌that makes gods gods: Indra drinks the soma press before every battle.
- **The Thousand-Eyed** — His body bears a thousand eyes — the marks of the gods’ curse ‌and his redemption; the sky’s innumerable lights.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Indra survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is ‌thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

No Indra temples survive in India — the Vedic cult was fire and libation, not ​image. But his name is carved across Southeast Asia: the seventh-century Sanskrit inscriptions of Cambodia invoke him as royal ancestor, and Borobudur’s reliefs show Śakra attending the Buddha.

## ​Realm & Domain

**Indra** is the king of the Vedic gods: the thunderbolt-bearer who slew the dragon Vritra and released the rivers, the drinker of soma who roars into ‌battle, the thousand-eyed lord of the sky. Two hundred and fifty hymns of the Rigveda are addressed to him — more than to any other deity — making him ​the best-documented god of the ancient world.

### The Vajra

The thunderbolt forged from the bones of the sage Dadhichi — Indra’s irresistible weapon against the dragon.

### Slayer of Vritra

​He split the dragon that held the waters captive, and the rivers ran free — the founding victory of cosmic order.

### Lord of Soma

The sacred draught that ‌makes gods gods: Indra drinks the soma press before every battle.

### The Thousand-Eyed

His body bears a thousand eyes — the marks of the gods’ curse and his redemption; ​the sky’s innumerable lights.

## Across Cultures

In Buddhism Indra becomes Śakra, lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, subservient to the Buddha and guardian of the dharma — the storm-god converted ​into a devotee. In Jainism he is a class of heaven-rulers. Greek observers heard Zeus in him; modern comparative philology confirmed the kinship: Indra and Zeus descend from the ‌same Proto-Indo-European sky-father’s thunderbolt.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[thor|Þórr]] (thunder sovereignty), [[zeus|Zeús]] (thunder sovereignty), [[adad|Adad]] (thunder / storm sovereignty), [[baal|Baꜥal]] (thunder / storm sovereignty), ​[[enlil|Enlīl]] (thunder / storm sovereignty), and [[illapa|Illapa]] (thunder / storm sovereignty).

## Cultural Legacy

He is embedded in the oldest Indo-European poetry extant — every study of dragon-slaying, thunder-gods, or ‌soma/haoma ritual begins with him. The word ‘Indra’ entered Southeast Asian royal names (Indravarman, Indrapura) carried by Hindu expansion; and the Vajra passed east into Tibetan Buddhism as the ​thunderbolt-sceptre of the vajrayāna itself.

## A Meditation

Indra: a name with no diacritics because it never needed any — ​the retroflex consonants of the Vedic hymns sit quietly inside plain letters, as they have since the first singer pressed soma. To restore him in ASCII is to hand ‌the thunderbolt back to the oldest god who still answers to the spelling a schoolchild would guess.

## The Canonical Spelling

**Indra** is the canonical spelling used by this temple. ‌The plain ASCII form *indra* contains the same letters, so there are no lost diacritics to recover and no special encoding transition to explain. A canonical name is a small map. In the case of **Indra**, the route does not lead through diacritics or ‌special letters, because the conventional scholarly spelling already uses the Latin alphabet. The original evidence — **इन्द्र** in Devanagari — carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can ​fully reproduce.

By fixing one reviewed spelling as the public reference, the project prevents the drift that occurs when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, ​and database. The character list shows exactly what is carried forward. "No change" here means a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and faithful to the record.
